lessons.title: Kinetic and Potential Energy: The Bucket in the Well

quiz.prompt: Mama Kavata lifts a full 20 kg bucket from the water at the bottom of an 8 m deep well to the ground at the top. What happens to the energy stored in the bucket because of its position as it is lifted?
choices: It increases, because the bucket is higher
It stays the same, because the bucket is the same bucket
It decreases, because the bucket is moving away from the water
It is zero all the time, because the bucket is not falling
quiz.rationale: The higher the bucket is lifted, the more energy it stores because of its position. This is the prediction the lesson aims to test against the evidence.
quiz.placement: Predict: Kitui story and prediction of how the bucket's energy changes from the water to the top

quiz.prompt: Mama Kavata lifts the 20 kg bucket 8 m by hand and finds it exhausting. Her daughter Mwende raises the same bucket the same 8 m using the pulley system and finds it easy. Which statement about the bucket at the top of the well is correct?
choices: The bucket has no stored energy for Mwende because she did not lift it by hand
The bucket has less stored energy for Mwende because it felt easier to lift
The bucket has the same stored energy at the top in both cases because it rose the same height
The bucket has more stored energy for Mwende because the pulley gave it extra energy
quiz.rationale: The bucket is the same and rises the same 8 m, so it gains the same stored energy either way. Feeling easier is about effort, not about the energy the bucket gains.
quiz.placement: Predict: question 'Will the energy gained be different for Mama Kavata and for Mwende?' and the prediction tally on the board

quiz.prompt: In the PhET Energy Skate Park simulation, a skater is released from the highest point of the track. At the moment the skater is at that highest point, which statement is correct?
choices: The skater's potential energy is greatest
The skater has no energy at all
The skater's potential energy and kinetic energy are both greatest
The skater's kinetic energy is greatest
quiz.rationale: At the highest point the skater is highest and has the most potential energy. The skater is about to start moving, so kinetic energy is low there.
quiz.placement: Observe: PhET Energy Skate Park, Task 2 (pause at the top, middle and bottom of the track)

quiz.prompt: In the PhET Energy Skate Park simulation, the skater slides down and reaches the lowest point of the track, moving fastest. What do the energy bars show at the lowest point?
choices: Potential energy is greatest and kinetic energy is lowest
Potential energy and kinetic energy are both zero
Kinetic energy is greatest and potential energy is lowest
Kinetic energy is lowest because the skater is at the bottom
quiz.rationale: At the bottom the skater is lowest, so potential energy is lowest, and fastest, so kinetic energy is greatest. Potential and kinetic energy trade off as the skater moves.
quiz.placement: Observe: PhET Energy Skate Park, Task 2 table (Position / Potential energy / Kinetic energy / Speed)

quiz.prompt: Which pair of statements correctly describes potential energy and kinetic energy?
choices: Potential energy is energy because of motion; kinetic energy is energy stored because of position
Potential energy is energy stored because of position; kinetic energy is energy an object has because it is moving
Potential energy is the force used to lift an object; kinetic energy is the effort a person feels
Potential energy is energy only for living things; kinetic energy is energy only for machines
quiz.rationale: Potential energy is stored because of position (such as a bucket high in the well) and kinetic energy is present because of motion. Energy is not the same as force or effort.
quiz.placement: Observe: vocabulary introduced after learners described the skater (potential and kinetic energy)

quiz.prompt: A bucket is lifted in an 8 m deep well. Its stored energy at each height is: 0 m (water) = 0 J, 2 m = 400 J, 4 m = 800 J, 6 m = 1200 J, 8 m (ground level) = 1600 J. Which pattern does this table show?
choices: The higher the bucket, the less potential energy it has
The potential energy stays the same at every height
The higher the bucket, the more potential energy it has
The potential energy is greatest at the water
quiz.rationale: The energy rises from 0 J to 1600 J as the height rises from 0 m to 8 m. Higher position means more stored potential energy.
quiz.placement: Observe: linking to the bucket using the bucket PE table (0, 400, 800, 1200, 1600 J)

quiz.prompt: Mwende finds the pulley makes lifting the bucket feel easier, even though the bucket rises the same 8 m. At this stage of the lesson, which statement is the best one to make about why the pulley makes it easier?
choices: The bucket stops having potential energy once it is on the pulley
The pulley makes the bucket lighter, so it stores less energy
The pulley adds extra energy to the bucket, so there is less to lift
We do not know yet; it is an open question for our Driving Question Board to investigate
quiz.rationale: This lesson only establishes that a higher bucket stores more potential energy. How the pulley helps, where the energy comes from and whether energy is lost are still open questions for later lessons.
quiz.placement: Explain and DQB: 'What might the pulley be doing?' and the 'We still wonder...' list on the Driving Question Board

lessons.title: Energy Transformations and the Formulas KE = ½mv² and PE = mgh

quiz.prompt: A 0.5 kg bob on a string is pulled up to one side and released so that it swings like a pendulum. Where is the bob moving fastest?
choices: It moves at the same speed everywhere
At the lowest point of the swing
At the highest point of the swing, where it starts
Half-way up either side of the swing
quiz.rationale: The bob loses height and so loses potential energy as it swings down. That energy becomes kinetic energy, so the speed is greatest at the lowest point. At the highest point the bob stops for an instant.
quiz.placement: Predict: bob held at a small height, 'Where is it fastest?'

quiz.prompt: A bob of mass 0.5 kg is raised 0.2 m above its lowest point. Using PE = mgh with g = 10 N/kg, what is its potential energy at the top?
choices: 1 J
quiz.rationale: PE = mgh = 0.5 x 10 x 0.2 = 1 J. Leaving out g gives 0.1 J. Using g = 9.8 gives 0.98 J, but this lesson uses g = 10 N/kg.
quiz.placement: Observe, Part A: pendulum, PE at top = mgh

quiz.prompt: The 0.5 kg bob passes the lowest point of its swing at a speed of 2 m/s. Using KE = ½mv², what is its kinetic energy there?
choices: 1 J
2 J
4 J
quiz.rationale: KE = ½mv² = ½ x 0.5 x 2² = ½ x 0.5 x 4 = 1 J. The common error is forgetting to square v, which gives 0.5 J.
quiz.placement: Observe, Part A: pendulum, KE at bottom = ½mv²

quiz.prompt: A roller coaster car of mass 1000 kg reaches the bottom of a hill at a speed of 20 m/s. Ignoring friction, what is its kinetic energy at the bottom?
quiz.rationale: KE = ½mv² = ½ x 1000 x 20² = ½ x 1000 x 400 = 200 000 J. Not squaring v gives 10 000 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 400 000 J.
quiz.placement: Observe, Part B: roller coaster, KE at the bottom with v = 20 m/s

quiz.prompt: A 20 kg bucket falls down a well from 8 m above the water surface. Ignoring friction, its PE at 8 m is 1600 J and its KE is 0 J. When it is 2 m above the water its PE is 400 J. What is its KE at this point?
quiz.rationale: The PE lost changes into KE. The bucket has lost 1600 - 400 = 1200 J of PE, so its KE is 1200 J. This matches the KE column of the table.
quiz.placement: Explain, Part A: PE and KE graph for the free-fall of the bucket

quiz.prompt: Mama Kavata lifts a 20 kg bucket (weight 200 N) by hand from the water surface to 8 m above it. Mwende lifts the same bucket the same 8 m using a pulley system. How much PE does the bucket gain in each case?
choices: 1600 J by hand and less than 1600 J with the pulley system
1600 J in both cases
1600 J by hand and more than 1600 J with the pulley system
800 J in both cases
quiz.rationale: The PE gain depends only on weight and height gained: 200 x 8 = 1600 J (or 20 x 10 x 8). The pulley does not appear in PE = mgh, so the gain is the same either way.
quiz.placement: Explain, Part C: PE gain of the bucket by hand or with the pulley system

quiz.prompt: After this lesson, which question about the bucket in the Kitui well is still NOT answered?
choices: How does PE change into KE when the bucket falls?
Which formula gives the PE of the bucket at a given height?
How much PE does the bucket gain when lifted 8 m?
Why does the pulley system feel easier to use when the bucket gains the same energy?
quiz.rationale: The lesson answered how much PE the bucket gains (1600 J), how energy changes form (PE to KE), and which formula to use (PE = mgh). It did not explain why the pulley needs less effort, so that question stays on the DQB.
quiz.placement: DQB: sorting questions into 'answered today', 'partly answered' and 'still to investigate'

lessons.title: Conservation of Energy: Does the Total Stay the Same? Pendulum and the Falling Bucket

quiz.prompt: A 20 kg bucket is released from the top of a well, 8 m above the water, and falls freely. Assume there is no friction or air resistance. As it falls, its PE goes down and its KE goes up. What happens to the TOTAL energy (KE + PE) of the bucket?
choices: It grows, because the bucket speeds up
It shrinks, because energy is used up as the bucket falls
It stays the same, because PE is changed into KE
It becomes zero when the bucket reaches the water
quiz.rationale: In an ideal system with no friction, energy is only transformed from PE to KE, so the total stays constant. The idea that energy is 'used up' or 'created' by motion is the common misconception.
quiz.placement: Predict: written predictions about the total (KE + PE) of the pendulum and the Kitui bucket, and the Prediction Wall

quiz.prompt: A 20 kg bucket is held 6 m above the water in a well. Use g = 10 N/kg. What is its potential energy (PE = mgh) relative to the water?
quiz.rationale: PE = mgh = 20 x 10 x 6 = 1200 J. The value 1176 J comes from using g = 9.8 N/kg, but this class uses g = 10 N/kg.
quiz.placement: Part B: completing the free-fall table for the 20 kg bucket released from 8 m

quiz.prompt: A 20 kg bucket is released from 8 m above the water, and there is no friction. When it is 2 m above the water, its PE is 400 J. Its total energy (KE + PE) is 1600 J at every height. What is its KE at 2 m? (Use g = 10 N/kg.)
quiz.rationale: Total = KE + PE, so KE = 1600 - 400 = 1200 J. The total of 1600 J comes from the starting PE of 20 x 10 x 8, which is 1600 J.
quiz.placement: Part B: adding the KE + PE column to the free-fall table and graphing PE, KE and total against height

quiz.prompt: A pendulum bob of mass 0.5 kg is pulled aside so that it is 0.2 m above its lowest point, and is then released. Assume there is no friction. Use g = 10 N/kg. When the bob is halfway down (0.1 m above its lowest point), what is its KE?
choices: 1 J
0 J
quiz.placement: Part A: PhET Pendulum Lab, recording PE, KE and total at the top, halfway down, bottom and halfway up

quiz.prompt: In the PhET Pendulum Lab, with friction set to NONE, a group sets the mass to 0.5 kg and raises the bob 0.2 m. They read a total energy of 0.98 J at every position, but they had calculated 1 J. What is the best explanation?
choices: Some energy is used up every time the bob swings
The simulation has lost 0.02 J of energy to friction
The total energy changes during the swing, so the reading is not constant
The simulation uses g = 9.8 N/kg, but we used g = 10 N/kg, so the total is constant but slightly different
quiz.rationale: 0.5 x 9.8 x 0.2 = 0.98 J, while 0.5 x 10 x 0.2 = 1 J. This is a difference in the value of g, not a change in energy, and the total stays constant.
quiz.placement: Part A: PhET Pendulum Lab, watching the total energy bar with friction set to NONE

quiz.prompt: Mwende lifts a 20 kg bucket 8 m up a well in Kitui, and the bucket gains 1600 J of PE. Energy cannot be created. Where does this 1600 J of energy come from?
choices: The chemical energy in her body, from food such as ugali and githeri
The energy comes from nowhere, since the bucket only changes position
The bucket makes its own energy as it moves upward
The rope and pulley create the extra energy
quiz.rationale: By conservation of energy, the bucket's gain in PE is transferred from the chemical energy stored in Mwende's body, which comes from her food. A pulley cannot create energy.
quiz.placement: Explain: applying the conservation principle to the Kitui phenomenon ('where did that 1600 J come from?')

quiz.prompt: A rubber band is stretched and then released, and it launches a small paper ball. Which statement best describes the energy changes?
choices: The energy is created at the moment of release
Elastic potential energy stored in the stretched rubber band changes into kinetic energy of the paper ball
The stretched rubber band has no stored energy, so the paper ball has KE only by chance
Kinetic energy in the rubber band changes into elastic potential energy of the ball
quiz.rationale: A stretched or compressed object stores elastic potential energy. When released, this changes into kinetic energy, following the same conservation idea.
quiz.placement: Explain: elastic potential energy demonstration with a rubber band launching a paper ball

lessons.title: Conservation of Energy in Applications: Where Does the Bucket's Energy Go in a Real Fall?

quiz.prompt: In Lesson 3, a 20 kg bucket released from 8 m in an ideal fall (no energy losses) hit the water at 12.6 m/s. A real bucket is now dropped down Mama Kavata's well in Kitui from the same 8 m. Which prediction is best?
choices: It hits the water at exactly 12.6 m/s, because the formula always works
It hits the water faster than 12.6 m/s, because the real well is deeper
It hits the water slower than 12.6 m/s, because some of its energy is transferred to heat, sound and friction
It hits the water slower than 12.6 m/s, because the energy is destroyed as it falls
quiz.rationale: In a real fall some energy goes to heat, sound and air/rope friction, so less is left as kinetic energy and the speed is lower. Energy is transferred, not destroyed.
quiz.placement: Predict: 'The bucket is dropped down the real well in Kitui. Will it hit the water at 12.6 m/s, faster, or slower?'

quiz.prompt: In a real fall, a 20 kg bucket reaches the water at 11 m/s. What is its kinetic energy at the water? (KE = 1/2 mv²)
quiz.rationale: KE = 1/2 × 20 × 11 × 11 = 1210 J. The wrong answers come from forgetting the half or the square, or from using the ideal value of 1600 J.
quiz.placement: Part A: data card of the real fall of the 20 kg bucket (calculating real KE at the bottom)

quiz.prompt: A 20 kg bucket starts from rest 8 m above the water. Using g = 10 N/kg, its PE at the top is 1600 J. In the real fall its KE at the water is 1210 J. How much energy was transferred to heat, sound and air/rope friction?
quiz.rationale: Total energy stays 1600 J, so the energy transferred to the surroundings = 1600 − 1210 = 390 J.
quiz.placement: Part A: filling in the Ideal versus Real table (difference = 1600 − 1210)

quiz.prompt: A block slides across a rough floor and stops. Just before stopping it had kinetic energy. Which statement best describes where that energy went?
choices: It changed into gravitational potential energy of the block
It was transferred to the floor, block and air as heat and sound
It went back into the block as extra kinetic energy
It was destroyed by friction
quiz.rationale: Friction transfers the block's kinetic energy to the surroundings as heat and sound, like the warmth felt when rubbing palms together. The energy is not destroyed.
quiz.placement: Part B: sliding demo (block on a rough floor, rubbing palms, 'Where did the motion energy of the block go when it stopped?')

quiz.prompt: A 2 kg block slides from rest down a smooth slope 0.5 m high. There is no friction. Using g = 10 N/kg, what is its speed at the bottom? (v = sqrt(2gh))
choices: 10 m/s
quiz.rationale: PE at the top = 2 × 10 × 0.5 = 10 J, which becomes 10 J of KE. So v = sqrt(2 × 10 × 0.5) = sqrt(10) ≈ 3.2 m/s. The mass cancels.
quiz.placement: Extra problem: 2 kg block sliding from rest down a smooth slope 0.5 m high

quiz.prompt: The same 2 kg block starts with 10 J of potential energy at the top of a slope. On a real, rough slope it reaches the bottom at 3.0 m/s. How much energy was transferred to heat and sound?
choices: 0 J
1 J
9 J
quiz.rationale: KE at the bottom = 1/2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 9 J. Energy transferred = 10 − 9 = 1 J.
quiz.placement: Extra problem: the real case where the block reaches the bottom at 3.0 m/s

quiz.prompt: A learner says: 'In the real fall of the bucket, the missing 390 J was destroyed by friction.' Which reply is correct?
choices: Energy is never destroyed: the 390 J was transferred to the surroundings as heat and sound, so 1600 J = 1210 J + 390 J
Wrong: the 390 J was turned back into potential energy at the top of the well
Wrong: the 390 J does not exist, because the real bucket has the same KE as the ideal bucket
Correct: friction uses up energy, so the total energy at the bottom is only 1210 J
quiz.rationale: Total energy is conserved. The bucket's 1600 J is shared between 1210 J of KE and 390 J transferred to heat, sound and air/rope friction.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning statement: 'The energy of the bucket was conserved' (correcting the 'energy destroyed' misconception)

lessons.title: Work: W = Fd – What Does Mama Kavata's Lift Really Do?

quiz.prompt: In physics, when is work done on an object?
choices: When a force acts on the object for a long time
When a person feels tired from pushing or holding the object
When a force moves the object in the direction of the force
When a person is busy doing a job such as farming
quiz.rationale: Work is done only when a force moves an object in the direction of the force (W = Fd). Tiredness or being busy is the everyday meaning of 'work', not the physics meaning.
quiz.placement: Predict: writing 'What do you think we mean by the word work in physics?'

quiz.prompt: Mama Kavata holds a 20 kg bucket still for 10 seconds. Her arms shake from the effort. How much work does she do on the bucket in the physics sense during this time?
choices: No work, because the bucket does not move
Negative work, because the bucket is not rising
Some work, because her arms are tired and shaking
Some work, because she is pulling upwards with 200 N
quiz.rationale: Work needs movement in the direction of the force. The bucket moves 0 m, so W = 200 N x 0 m = 0 J, even though her muscles are tired.
quiz.placement: Predict: 'Mama Kavata holds the bucket still for 10 seconds with her arms shaking. Does she do work on the bucket?'

quiz.prompt: In the Mini-Well investigation, a learner lifts a 2 kg load (weight 20 N) slowly and steadily 1 m from the floor onto a bench. How much work does the learner do on the load?
choices: 2 J
quiz.rationale: The lifting force equals the weight, 20 N, and the distance moved upwards is 1 m. W = Fd = 20 N x 1 m = 20 J.
quiz.placement: Observe: Mini-Well lifting investigation (2 kg load raised 1 m)

quiz.prompt: A learner lifts a 2 kg load onto a bench, then carries it 2 m sideways at a steady height. During the sideways carry, the learner's lifting force is upwards but the motion is horizontal. How much work does the lifting force do on the load during the sideways carry?
choices: 40 J, because 20 N x 2 m = 40 J
Negative work, because the force is opposite to the motion
0 J, because the force is at right angles to the motion
20 J, because the load is still being held up
quiz.rationale: The upward lifting force is at right angles to the horizontal motion, so there is no distance moved in the direction of the force. The work done by the lifting force is 0 J.
quiz.placement: Observe: carrying the load 2 m horizontally at a steady height

quiz.prompt: Mama Kavata lifts a bucket of weight 200 N steadily up through 4 m of the well. Using W = Fd, how much work does she do on the bucket over these 4 m?
quiz.rationale: W = Fd = 200 N x 4 m = 800 J. This matches the gain in potential energy of the bucket at 4 m.
quiz.placement: Observe: bucket data table, computing F x d for 2 m, 4 m, 6 m and 8 m and comparing with the PE column

quiz.prompt: Mama Kavata lifts a 20 kg bucket (weight 200 N) steadily up an 8 m deep well. What is the work done by gravity on the bucket during the lift?
choices: -200 J, because the weight is 200 N
0 J, because the bucket moves at steady speed
+1600 J, because gravity acts on the bucket the whole time
-1600 J, because gravity's force is opposite to the motion
quiz.rationale: Gravity pulls down with 200 N while the bucket moves up 8 m, so the force is opposite to motion. W = -200 N x 8 m = -1600 J.
quiz.placement: Explain: sign table (gravity 200 N down while the bucket goes up)

quiz.prompt: During the steady 8 m lift of a 200 N bucket, the woman does +1600 J of work and gravity does -1600 J of work. What is the net work on the bucket, and what does it tell us?
choices: 3200 J, so the bucket's speed keeps increasing
-1600 J, so the bucket loses energy
0 J, so the bucket's kinetic energy does not change and its speed stays constant
0 J, so nothing happened to the bucket
quiz.rationale: Net work = +1600 + (-1600) = 0 J. With no net work, KE and speed stay constant, even though the bucket's PE rises by 1600 J.
quiz.placement: Explain: sign table, net work = +1600 + (-1600) = 0 J

quiz.prompt: Mama Kavata now lowers the 200 N bucket slowly down 8 m using a rope. Her pull on the rope is upwards. What is the work done by the woman?
choices: -1600 J, because her force is up while the motion is down
+1600 J, because she is still pulling with 200 N
-200 J, because the force is 200 N
0 J, because the bucket is not being lifted
quiz.rationale: Her force is upwards and the bucket moves downwards, so force and motion are opposite. W = -200 N x 8 m = -1600 J. Negative work takes energy away from the bucket.
quiz.placement: Explain: lowering the bucket slowly 8 m by rope (signs reversed)

quiz.prompt: A farmer in the Rift Valley pushes a wheelbarrow with a steady force of 60 N along a straight path through 10 m, in the direction of the push. How much work does the farmer do on the wheelbarrow?
choices: 6 J
quiz.rationale: The force and motion are in the same direction, so W = Fd = 60 N x 10 m = 600 J.
quiz.placement: Explain: quick problem on the farmer pushing a wheelbarrow

quiz.prompt: A learner says: 'The work done by the woman on the bucket is negative, so no work is done and the energy is wasted.' Which statement best corrects this idea?
choices: Negative work means the force and motion are opposite, and it takes energy away from the object
Negative work means the energy is lost as heat
Negative work means the object has stopped moving
Negative work means the force is smaller than the weight
quiz.rationale: A negative sign shows that force and motion are in opposite directions. Positive work gives energy to an object and negative work takes energy away; it does not mean no work or wasted energy.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: clarifying the misconception that negative work means no work or wasted energy

lessons.title: Work and Energy: Hand Lift versus Pulley System at the Kitui Well

quiz.prompt: At a well in Kitui, Mama Kavata lifts a 20 kg bucket of water (weight 200 N) straight up 8 m by hand at a steady speed. How much work does she do on the bucket?
quiz.rationale: Work = force x distance = 200 N x 8 m = 1600 J. The other values come from multiplying the mass by the distance, adding the numbers, or dividing them.
quiz.placement: Predict: how would we calculate the work Mama Kavata does when she lifts the bucket by hand?

quiz.prompt: A 20 kg bucket is raised 8 m up a well, once by hand and once using a pulley system that needs a smaller pulling force. Which statement about the energy gained by the bucket is correct?
choices: It is zero in both cases, because the bucket moves at a steady speed.
It is more with the pulley, because the pulley adds extra energy.
It is the same both ways, because the bucket rises the same height.
It is less with the pulley, because the pulling force is smaller.
quiz.rationale: The bucket's energy gain depends on its weight and the height it rises (the gain in PE), not on the method used. Less effort does not mean less energy gained, and a pulley does not create energy.
quiz.placement: Predict: bar-chart sketch of 'energy given by the person' and 'energy gained by the bucket' for each method

quiz.prompt: In a model lift, a learner pulls a string over a two-pulley arrangement with a steady effort of 12 N. The string moves 0.8 m while the 2 kg mass rises 0.4 m. How much work does the learner do on the string?
quiz.rationale: Work input = effort x distance the string moves = 12 N x 0.8 m = 9.6 J. This is more than the 8 J (20 N x 0.4 m) needed to lift the mass directly, because of friction.
quiz.placement: Part A: model lift with spring balance, string and two pulleys

quiz.prompt: With the pulley system at the Kitui well, Mwende pulls the rope with a steady force of 125 N through 16 m. The 20 kg bucket gains 1600 J of potential energy. How much energy is transferred as heat by friction in the pulleys and rope?
choices: 0 J
quiz.rationale: Work input = 125 N x 16 m = 2000 J. Energy transferred as heat = 2000 J - 1600 J = 400 J.
quiz.placement: Part B: Kitui data (hand lift 1600 J, pulley system 2000 J, difference 400 J)

quiz.prompt: Why does the pulley system feel easier for Mwende than lifting the bucket by hand?
choices: It makes the bucket lighter, so its weight is smaller.
It reduces the work needed to lift the bucket, so the bucket gains less energy.
It gives the bucket extra energy that comes from the pulleys.
It needs a smaller force, but the rope is pulled over a longer distance.
quiz.rationale: The pulley system trades force for distance: 125 N over 16 m instead of 200 N over 8 m. The bucket still gains 1600 J, and its weight is unchanged.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: why the pulley system feels easier even though the bucket gains the same energy

quiz.prompt: Mwende does 2000 J of work with the pulley system, but the bucket gains only 1600 J of potential energy. What happens to the other 400 J?
choices: It is destroyed by the pulleys.
It is transferred to the surroundings as heat (and a little sound) by friction.
It is stored in the bucket as extra kinetic energy.
It is stored in the bucket as extra potential energy.
quiz.rationale: Energy is conserved. Friction in the pulleys and rope transfers the 400 J to the surroundings as heat and a little sound. The bucket moves at a steady speed, so its KE does not change.
quiz.placement: Sankey-style energy-flow diagram: where is the other 400 J?

quiz.prompt: In the Kitui pulley system, 400 J of the 2000 J of work input is transferred as heat. What percentage of the work input is this?
quiz.rationale: Percentage = 400 J / 2000 J x 100 = 20%. A learner who divides by 1600 J instead of the input gets 25%.
quiz.placement: Explain: note that 400 J is 20% of the input

lessons.title: Work Against Friction and Power: Dragging the Maize Sack and Lifting Water

quiz.prompt: A 50 kg sack of maize weighs 500 N. It is dragged 10 m across a rough dirt yard and then 10 m across a smooth concrete floor, both at steady speed. The friction force is 150 N on the dirt and 100 N on the concrete. Why does dragging it across the dirt need more work?
choices: The sack is dragged a longer distance on the dirt
The friction force is larger on the dirt, so work = friction × distance is larger
The sack gains more potential energy on the dirt
The sack weighs more on the dirt than on the concrete
quiz.rationale: The weight (500 N) and the distance (10 m) are the same on both surfaces. The rough dirt gives a larger friction force (150 N against 100 N), so W = f × d is larger (1500 J against 1000 J).
quiz.placement: Part A: friction investigation (homestead data for the 50 kg sack, rough dirt and smooth concrete)

quiz.prompt: A 50 kg sack is dragged 10 m at steady speed across a rough dirt yard. The friction force is 150 N. How much work is done to drag the sack?
quiz.rationale: At steady speed the pulling force equals friction, so W = F × d = 150 N × 10 m = 1500 J.
quiz.placement: Part A: friction investigation (computing W = Fd for the rough surface)

quiz.prompt: A sack is dragged along level ground at steady speed. It does not rise, and it does not speed up. What happens to the energy used to drag it?
choices: It is stored as potential energy in the sack
It is destroyed because the sack gains no height
It becomes kinetic energy that makes the sack move faster
It is transferred to the surroundings as heat because of friction
quiz.rationale: The sack gains no PE and no KE. The work done against friction is transferred as heat to the sack, the ground and the air. Energy is not destroyed.
quiz.placement: Part A: friction investigation (where did the 1500 J go if the sack did not rise?)

quiz.prompt: A 50 kg learner climbs a flight of stairs by running, doing 1500 J of work in 3 s. What is the learner's power?
quiz.rationale: Power = work ÷ time = 1500 J ÷ 3 s = 500 W.
quiz.placement: Part B: power (stair-climb data, running 3 s)

quiz.prompt: Two learners of the same mass climb the same stairs. The walker takes 6 s and the runner takes 3 s. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both do the same work, but the runner has more power
Both do the same work and have the same power
The runner does more work and has more power
The walker does more work because the walker takes longer
quiz.rationale: Both lift the same mass through the same height, so the work is the same (1500 J). Power is the rate of doing work (P = W/t), so the runner, who takes less time, has the greater power.
quiz.placement: Explain: exit question (runner and walker climb the same stairs)

quiz.prompt: Mama Kavata lifts a 20 kg bucket of water from an 8 m deep well by hand, which needs 1600 J of work. She takes 40 s instead of 20 s. What is her power?
quiz.rationale: P = W ÷ t = 1600 J ÷ 40 s = 40 W. This is half of the 80 W she has when she does the same work in 20 s.
quiz.placement: Explain: short problem (2) on the second 20 kg bucket lifted in 40 s

quiz.prompt: A pulley system needs 2000 J of work input to raise a bucket of water that gains 1600 J of potential energy. Where does the extra 400 J go?
choices: It is stored as extra potential energy in the water
It is destroyed by the pulley
It is given back to the person pulling the rope
It is transferred as heat, mainly by friction in the pulleys and rope
quiz.rationale: Friction in the pulleys and rope opposes motion, so some of the input work is transferred to the surroundings as heat (2000 J − 1600 J = 400 J). Energy is never destroyed.
quiz.placement: Model Building: adding 2000 J in, 1600 J to PE and 400 J to heat by friction on the Kitui bucket model

lessons.title: Simple Machines, MA, VR, Efficiency and the Final Model: Why the Pulley Makes the Bucket Feel Light

quiz.prompt: At the pulley station, a 200 N bucket of water is lifted using a pulley system. The effort needed is 125 N. What is the mechanical advantage (MA = load/effort) of the pulley system?
quiz.rationale: MA = load / effort = 200 N / 125 N = 1.6. Dividing effort by load gives the inverted value 0.625, and 80 is the efficiency in per cent, not the MA.
quiz.placement: Station 1 Pulley system: load 200 N, effort 125 N

quiz.prompt: Two youths load a 50 kg sack of maize (weight 500 N) onto a lorry 1.0 m high using a 4 m plank as a ramp. They push with an effort of 200 N along the plank. Using efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100%, what is the efficiency of the ramp?
quiz.rationale: MA = 500/200 = 2.5 and VR = 4/1 = 4, so efficiency = (2.5/4) x 100% = 62.5%. The work output is 500 J and the work input is 800 J, which also gives 62.5%.
quiz.placement: Station 2 Ramp: 50 kg sack loaded 1.0 m high with a 4 m plank

quiz.prompt: A farmer uses a crowbar to lift a heavy stone. The effort is 125 N and the load is 400 N. The effort arm is 1.2 m and the load arm is 0.3 m. What is the mechanical advantage of the crowbar?
quiz.rationale: MA = load / effort = 400 N / 125 N = 3.2. The value 4 is the velocity ratio (1.2 m / 0.3 m), and 0.3125 comes from dividing effort by load.
quiz.placement: Station 3 Lever (crowbar): effort arm 1.2 m, load arm 0.3 m, load 400 N, effort 125 N

quiz.prompt: Mwende uses a single fixed pulley (one wheel fixed above the well) to lift a 200 N bucket. Which statement is correct?
choices: The velocity ratio is 2, so the effort is halved to 100 N.
The pulley reduces the work needed to lift the bucket.
The pulley gives the bucket extra energy so it rises more easily.
The velocity ratio is 1, so the effort is still about 200 N and the pulley only changes the direction of the force.
quiz.rationale: A single fixed pulley has VR = 1, so the ideal effort equals the load (200 N). It only changes the direction, which lets Mwende pull down using her body weight.
quiz.placement: Station 1 Pulley system: single fixed pulley alone has VR = 1

quiz.prompt: A bucket gains 1600 J of potential energy. With the pulley system, Mwende pulls the rope with a 125 N effort over 16 m. How much of the energy she supplies is transferred as heat by friction in the pulleys and rope?
choices: 0 J, because energy cannot be lost
quiz.rationale: Work input = 125 N x 16 m = 2000 J. Output is 1600 J of PE, so 2000 - 1600 = 400 J is transferred as heat by friction. Energy is not destroyed, so it is conserved.
quiz.placement: Final Explanation (CER): 1600 J becomes PE and 400 J (20%) is transferred as heat by friction

quiz.prompt: A woman lifts a 20 kg bucket 8 m by hand. A child lifts the same bucket the same height using a pulley system. Which statement best explains why the pulley system feels easier?
choices: The pulley system gives the bucket extra energy.
The bucket gains less potential energy with the pulley system.
The pulley system needs a smaller force but over a longer distance, so the work is not reduced.
The pulley system reduces the work needed, so less energy is used.
quiz.rationale: The bucket gains the same PE either way. A machine trades a smaller force for a longer distance (effort 125 N over 16 m instead of 200 N over 8 m) and never reduces the work needed. Friction means slightly more work is actually done.
quiz.placement: Final Explanation (CER): the pulley trades a smaller force for a longer distance (VR = 2, MA = 1.6)

quiz.prompt: An ideal pulley system with no friction has a velocity ratio of 2 and is used to lift a 200 N bucket. Its efficiency would be 100%, so MA = VR. What effort is needed?
quiz.rationale: With 100% efficiency, MA = VR = 2. Effort = load / MA = 200 N / 2 = 100 N. The real pulley system needs 125 N because of friction.
quiz.placement: Challenge: could an ideal pulley system with no friction have 100% efficiency?

quiz.prompt: Mwende, a 10-year-old, lifts the bucket with the pulley system. Where does the energy she supplies come from originally?
choices: From chemical energy stored in food such as ugali and githeri
From the friction in the rope
From the pulley system, which creates energy
From the potential energy of the bucket at the bottom of the well
quiz.rationale: The energy Mwende supplies comes from chemical energy in the food she has eaten. The pulley only transfers energy and does not create it, and friction transfers some energy to heat.
quiz.placement: Final model: source of energy (chemical energy from ugali or githeri in Mama Kavata or Mwende)
